    LLMs vs SLMs: scale, cost, latency

    After this lesson you can reason about the trade-off between large and small models in concrete terms — memory, latency, cost — and explain when a fine-tuned small model is the right choice over a frontier LLM.

    Level: beginner Read time: ~9 min Prerequisites: Pretraining vs fine-tuning vs prompting vs RAG Verified: 13 Nov 2026

    "Large" and "small" language models run on the exact same machinery you've now seen — tokens, embeddings, Transformer blocks, next-token prediction. The difference is one number: the parameter count. That single number cascades into memory, speed, cost, and capability, and understanding the cascade tells you which model to reach for.

    The one axis: parameters

    Model size is measured in parameters: a small model like SmolLM2 has ~135 million, and this course calls anything up to roughly 10 billion small; frontier models run from hundreds of billions to over a trillion total parameters, often as a mixture of experts that uses only a fraction of them for each token. More parameters means more capacity to absorb patterns during pretraining, which is why the biggest models display the broadest knowledge and strongest general reasoning.

    But every parameter has to be stored and multiplied on every token. So scale is not free.

    What scale costs: memory, latency, money

    • Memory (VRAM). Parameters live in GPU memory. A rough rule: bytes ≈ parameters × bytes-per-parameter. At 2 bytes each (bf16), a 135M model needs ~0.27 GB just for weights; a 70B model needs ~140 GB — many GPUs. Full fine-tuning needs several times more: about 16 bytes per parameter with the usual mixed-precision AdamW setup (weights, gradients and optimizer state), before activations (a rule of thumb from the ZeRO paper, Rajbhandari et al. 2019, arXiv 1910.02054; the exact figure depends on the optimizer and precision; Lesson 1.15's memory table breaks it down). That is why fine-tuning a giant model is a data-center activity and fine-tuning an SLM fits on one consumer GPU.
    • Latency. Generating each token runs the whole network. More parameters → more arithmetic per token → slower responses. Small models reply faster, which matters for interactive and high-volume use. A useful upper bound: generating one token at a time, a model must read all its weights from memory for each token, so tokens per second ≈ memory bandwidth ÷ bytes of weights read per token. Worked example on a GPU with 1,000 GB/s of memory bandwidth: SmolLM2-135M in bf16 is 0.27 GB, so at most about 1,000 ÷ 0.27 ≈ 3,700 tokens/s; a 7B model in bf16 is 14 GB, so at most about 70 tokens/s. Real numbers are lower (the KV cache and other overheads are also read), so treat this as a ceiling, not a forecast.
    • Cost. Whether you pay an API per token or rent a GPU per hour, cost tracks compute, which tracks size. A task served billions of times is dramatically cheaper on a small model.

    What small models give up — and what they don't

    Out of the box, a small model knows less and reasons less broadly. Ask a 135M base model open-ended trivia and it will disappoint. That's the honest downside.

    But most production work is not open-ended. It's one narrow, repeated task: classify this ticket, extract these fields, answer questions about these docs, rewrite in this format. For a narrow task, broad knowledge is mostly wasted — and this is the crux:

    The thesis of this course

    On a single, well-defined task, a fine-tuned small model can match a model hundreds of times larger, at a fraction of the cost and latency, running on hardware you control. Fine-tuning concentrates a small model's limited capacity onto your task. "Can" is the honest word: it fails when the task needs broad knowledge, long multi-step reasoning or facts the model never saw, and you only find out by measuring. In one of our own projects the fine-tune lost to retrieval.

    When to pick which

    • Pick a large general model when you need broad, open-ended capability, low volume, and don't want to train anything — a do-everything assistant, exploratory work, or the first prototype.
    • Pick a fine-tuned small model when you have one repeatable task at meaningful volume, care about cost/latency/privacy, or need to run locally/offline. This is BrewSLM's target: take a small base, fine-tune it on your data, and ship something cheap and fast that's good enough — and then prove it's good enough. BrewSLM's SLM-vs-frontier report does exactly this: it compares your model with a frontier model evaluated on the same eval set, and puts cost and latency next to quality. The Track 4 capstone shows how to stack that evidence into a ship decision.

    A useful habit

    Frame the decision as quality-per-dollar (or per-millisecond) for your task, not quality in the abstract. A model that's 95% as good at 2% of the cost is usually the better engineering choice (a heuristic: it depends on what the missing 5% costs you) — and you can only know those numbers by evaluating, which is why evaluation gets its own lessons.

    Where we go next

    You now have the whole mental model: what a model is, how it learns, how text becomes math, how the Transformer and next-token prediction produce language, the four levers for steering a model, and why small models are worth fine-tuning. The next lesson zooms all the way out to the shape of a real SLM project — the loop you'll execute for the rest of the course.

    Recap

    • LLMs and SLMs share the same machinery; the difference is the parameter count, and this course calls up to roughly 10B "small".
    • Size drives memory (≈ params × bytes per param for weights, about 16 bytes per param for full fine-tuning), latency (bounded by bandwidth ÷ bytes read per token) and cost.
    • A fine-tuned SLM can match a much larger model on one narrow task, and can also lose; only a measured comparison on your task tells you which.

    Try it (5 minutes)

    You are sizing a 1.7B model for a GPU with 24 GB of memory and 300 GB/s of bandwidth. (1) How much memory do the bf16 weights need, and what is the decode ceiling in tokens/s at batch size 1? (2) Same questions for a 4-bit version (about 0.5 bytes per parameter). (3) Does full fine-tuning in mixed-precision AdamW fit, by the 16-bytes rule?

    Show answer

    (1) 1.7B × 2 bytes = 3.4 GB; 300 ÷ 3.4 ≈ 88 tokens/s at most. (2) 1.7B × 0.5 bytes ≈ 0.85 GB (a little more in practice, for scales and unquantised layers); 300 ÷ 0.85 ≈ 350 tokens/s at most. (3) 1.7B × 16 bytes ≈ 27 GB before activations, so no: it does not fit in 24 GB. That is why Track 1 reaches for LoRA, which trains a small adapter and keeps the base weights frozen.

    Key terms

    Parameter count
    The number of weights in a model; the primary axis of "size."
    Small language model (SLM)
    A model with relatively few parameters (up to roughly 10 billion; this course uses 135 million).
    VRAM
    GPU memory; weights need ≈ params × bytes-per-param, full fine-tuning about 16 bytes per parameter plus activations.
    Latency
    Time to produce output; rises with model size since each token runs the whole network.
    Memory bandwidth
    How fast the GPU reads memory; at batch size 1, tokens/s ≤ bandwidth ÷ bytes of weights read per token.
    Cost per token
    The price of generating output, which tracks compute and therefore size.
    Narrow vs general task
    A single repeatable job vs open-ended capability; narrow tasks favor fine-tuned SLMs.
